details.title: Arban – Slur Study No. 27
details.lead: From Arban's Grande méthode complète de cornet à pistons et de saxhorn, first edition, 1864. The notes are the cornet part as printed, in written pitch for the B♭ cornet. Below: the book's own words, translated from the French.
facts: Arban, Grande méthode complète de cornet à pistons et de saxhorn, first edition (Paris: Léon Escudier, 1864)
The book prints the second and third bar of each figure as repeat signs; written out here.

sections.heading: Studies on the slur
paragraphs: This part of the method is beyond question one of the most important, and so I have given it a great deal of room, above all in the exercises played only by the movement of the lips, that is, without adding or changing a valve. The fingerings shown must be followed exactly, unusual as they are. I chose them on purpose: not to recommend them for everyday playing, but to give this kind of exercise a difficulty that absolutely must be overcome, by forcing the lips to move without the help of the valves.
This work is much like the work singers do when they study the movement of the glottis in order to trill.
The easiest interval to slur is the minor second. The major second is a little harder, for it already needs a certain movement of the lips.
The third is the hardest, because it often falls on degrees where the valves cannot help carry the sound from the low note to the high one.
So I advise working hard at this kind of exercise. It becomes the source of an easy and brilliant execution, and it gives the lips great suppleness, above all once you can reach the trill.

The trill made with the lips is good only for intervals where the harmonics lie a second apart, as in exercise No. 23, and above all when the fingerings shown are followed; otherwise you would make trills of thirds, which would be as unpleasant as they are bad.

I give these exercises only as studies, and I do not at all urge pupils to use them in performance, as certain horn players do who want to bring to the cornet a system that has no reason to exist on it. The cornet is one of the most perfect and complete of instruments; it rejects, rather than needs, artificial tricks whose effect will always seem detestable to people of taste.
Here I must point out one more intolerable habit that the followers of this school of lip movement seem to love. I mean the way they play the gruppetto.
To play this ornament on the cornet it is enough to move the fingers evenly, and every note comes out perfectly in tune and clean.

By what right, then, do certain players replace with a third above the appoggiatura that should be a second away? Why, in a word, do they play Example 1 instead of Example 2, which is the only proper way, and this on every degree of the scale? Because these gentlemen find it easier to fall back on a simple movement of the lips that spares them moving their fingers; as if it were not more natural to bring out the true notes with the valves.
Along this road some go further still, and do not hesitate to play runs of triplets by moving the lips instead of using the valves.
An example from a study by M. Gallay. It must be played as in Example 3, with the valves, instead of with the lips, which gives the execrable effect of Example 4.

I need not say more to show that such sleight of hand has no reason to exist on the cornet. If I mention it here, it is only to put the pupil on guard against a system that is, unhappily, too widespread in the army.

The first fifteen numbers of this part have only one aim: to teach how to carry the sound. To do it, swell the low note a little, and at the moment it reaches its full strength carry it to the high note by a light pressure of the mouthpiece on the lips.

Then comes the work on the third, which is obtained by tensing the muscles and also by the pressure of the mouthpiece on the lips. Make every note speak very evenly, binding the notes well together and following the rhythms and fingerings shown.

All the studies from No. 16 to No. 69 are written only to learn to carry thirds with ease, so as to pass gracefully through the small grace notes and the double appoggiaturas. I have already added a few examples of these to this series; they will be treated fully later, in the chapter on ornaments.
As these two ornaments are obtained only by the movement of the lips, I thought I should give some applications of them here.
